crux.for_the_english: Keep the comic disproportion intact. Do not make Taki's inner language beautiful and the pond business merely coarse background, and do not make the narration wink at him from outside. The same English must be able to inflate a carp-hunt into a battle, a chorus, a theatrical tableau, and then let it collapse into mud, cicadas and an unpaid bill. His quoted-back phrases — “the difficult work I'm holding in my head!”, “in one burst!”, “Nancy Lee”, “the telephone!”, “the terrifying blizzard!”, “nothing but a snowscape to look at!” — should recur recognisably, because in p160 the narration throws his own slogans back at him as they all scatter 'like goose down' while he sits glaring at the pond.
crux.point: The gap between Taki's cherished, unwritten inner work and the squalid, absorbing business that actually fills his days — and the way the narration keeps lending the second the epic language of the first.
crux.why: Taki is a writer who has not really begun: he tells his wife the work is 'about half' done (p28) when in fact, once he took up his pen, he could write it 'in one burst' at any time — or so he believes; putting it into prose feels to him as clumsy and roundabout as making conversation. Everything grand in the story stays in his head, in quotation marks. Everything that actually happens is petty and physical: a pond dug for no good reason, carp that cannot be caught, a house about to be demolished and replaced by a warehouse, a telephone he suddenly decides to sell, carp suddenly worth four hundred yen, creditors at the door. The story's energy is the traffic between the two. His wife's casual remark that his finished seascape looks 'like a snowscape, in midsummer' (p58) detonates a paragraph of self-laceration in which all his realistic fiction and his whole foolish way of living become a botched 'snowscape', a blizzard rises, and he must flee across a white wilderness (p61–62). By section III the same man is bellowing orders at two workmen in a muddy pond like a general, then like an impresario inviting spectators up to the best seats, then discovering that this is more fun than any pleasure he knows (p165–179). In section IV the pumping-out of the pond, done by his assembled creditors, acquires 'the same underlying force as the chorus of Nancy Lee' (p210) — the sentimental whaling song he inherited from his father — while Taki himself is simply absent, gone to Tokyo 'to buy a lamp' (p212). If a translation resolves this into satire on a lazy writer, or into lyrical sympathy for a dreamer, it has chosen one pole and lost the story.

open_questions.question: What exactly has Taki produced in the 'finished' sketch, and how literally should the snow vision be taken? The text never shows us the picture; we have only his wife's puzzled remark and his disproportionate reaction. Is the sketch a failed seascape, an accidental near-abstract, or an honest rendering of how dazzled eyes see a midsummer shore? The translation should preserve the fact that we never see it directly — but the degree of visual oddity implied in 'like a snowscape' affects how strange the English should let the phrase sound.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The title hangs on this unseen picture. Over-explaining it (a bad painting, a visionary one, a hallucination) settles the story's central uncertainty.

open_questions.question: How much of the father's whaling-ship past is family myth? The father 'said' he shipped on a whaler in his American schooldays and learned Nancy Lee from the sailors; Taki repeats this as fact, but the whole anecdote has the shine of a story told too often and too theatrically, with gestures. Should the English keep a faint hearsay colouring ('he used to say...') or report it straight?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The song, and the father's romantic self-image, are Taki's one inherited piece of 'the sea'; whether he is heir to an adventure or to a performance bears on how we hear his own performances in section III.

open_questions.question: Is Taki's final absence from the pumping of the pond evasion, indifference, or the story's quiet verdict — that the work of his life will be done by other people, for money he owes, while he is elsewhere on an errand? The last line gives only the caretaker's report ('gone to Tokyo to buy a lamp'). Should the English let that stand as flatly as the Japanese does, with no closing cadence supplied?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Any added point or rounding-off in the final sentence would manufacture an ending the text refuses; but how bare 'to buy a lamp' sounds in English decides whether the refusal reads as design or as a translation gap.

open_questions.question: Why do Taki and his wife live in separate houses, and what is the temperature of the marriage? The text gives only glancing evidence: she comes looking for him, teases him, fears he will join the workmen's drinking, rings the caretaker to intercept him. Is this estrangement, a workable arrangement, or a wife managing a hopeless husband at arm's length?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Her lines can be played cold, affectionate or exasperated, and English dialogue will force a choice line by line; the reading above assumes affection worn into exasperation, but the text never confirms it.

data.reading:
The crux comes first. Taki lives by a phrase: 'in one burst!' (一気呵勢, p74). It is his motto, his excuse and his sedative — having thought it, he can become 'easily optimistic', make himself a little more leisure, and sink back into the 'dream'. The story is built as a series of occasions on which that leisure gets filled by something else, each time more completely. First a walk to escape the oppressiveness of thinking about fiction (p2); then his wife's arrival and the long, circling conversation about the carp, the doomed house, the trip they will supposedly take, the house they will supposedly rent in Tokyo (p3–p48); then the detonation of the 'snowscape' remark; then drink, the telephone inspiration, the carp valuation, the brothel; then the hunt itself, which swallows an entire day and remakes him as 'a haughty bourgeois waiting for his prey' (p160); finally the creditors pumping the pond dry in heroic unison while he is not there. Nothing in his life is ever quite refused — the trip is always about to happen, his mother may join them whenever she likes, the work is always half done — and the English must keep that soft, agreeable evasiveness in the dialogue. Taki's characteristic move is the answer that sounds like agreement and commits him to nothing ('Go if you like', p30, at once corrected, too late, to 'I want to go'), and the narration itself notices the habit (p33). If his lines are made decisive, or his wife's made merely nagging, the marriage — two people who have long practice at not quite meeting — disappears.

Register is where a fluent draft will most reliably go wrong, because the text runs on at least four distinct musics and keeps cutting between them without warning. There is the narration in a literary Taishō-Shōwa written style, capable of a level, almost reportorial calm (the opening walk, the still noon tableau of p180–181, where the two workmen freeze like figures in a play and a bubble bursts on the mud). There is Taki's interior weather: rhymed, 'poetic' reverie (韻文的な想ひ) that tips without a seam into self-parody — the snow passage of p61–62 is the extreme case, moving from an owl's eyes in daylight to sinful snowflakes 'the size of peony petals' burying his body, all triggered by a wife's mild puzzlement and punctured at once by her 'What's the matter?' and his sheepish change of subject (p63–66). There is the wife's speech: quick, Tokyo, feminine in the period's inflections, teasing and managerial at once, the only voice in the story that consistently says what things cost and what will actually happen. And there are A and B, the tattooed workmen, whose pond-side talk (p40–47) is broad working-class vernacular — boastful, sweaty, obscene round the edges — set down with evident relish by the narrator, who even pauses to describe their tattoos (the completed dragon; the unfinished hannya mask, and Taki's unasked question about why it was abandoned, p48). The temptation is to level these into one pleasant literary voice, or to render the workmen in some borrowed English dialect that pins them to a place they never lived. Resist both. They should sound rougher, faster and funnier than everyone else without turning into music-hall turns; Taki should sound smoother and vaguer than everyone else without turning into a poet.

The comedy is deadpan and structural, and it lives in repetition. Catch the carp: the word つかまへる tolls through the story from the wife's first line (p5) through the workmen's laments to Taki's bellowing 'the net! the net! the net!' (p166), and the pond obligingly clouds every time anyone moves — a small, perfect mechanism of frustration that the English should let recur in the same plain words rather than varying into 'grab', 'land', 'net' by turns. Likewise 'in one burst', which migrates grotesquely from Taki's unwritten masterpiece (p74) to A and B's plan to pump the pond dry 'in one burst' (p206): the same slogan, finally attached to the only decisive act in the book, performed by his creditors. Nancy Lee travels the same road, from the father's deck-song, through Taki's solitary whistling and his wife's ostentatious ear-covering (p104–106), to the straining chorus of the pump-handlers (p210) — the one moment of genuine collective vigour in the story, and it belongs to the men he owes money. Keep the song's title untranslated and unexplained in the text; its slight foreign quaintness in 1927 Japan is part of the point, and the wife's objection that an American sailors' song is old and vulgar should be allowed to stand against Taki's sentimentality without the narration adjudicating. The same deadpan applies to money, which a fluent version may be tempted to keep vague: ten yen produced from a wife's purse, four hundred yen for carp, month-end bills, the telephone as a saleable asset. The amounts are the story's ballast.

What the text leaves unsaid should stay unsaid. Subjects drop for sentences at a time; dialogue goes unattributed (notably the restaurant haggling, p108–120, and the drunken walk home, p121–146, where Taki's parenthesised realisations — the telephone! it's mine! I'll sell it! — interrupt the old caretaker's patter and should stay typographically and rhythmically separate, a drunk man's lightning inside a slow scene). The unfinished things are thematic, not accidental: the unfinished tattoo, the unfinished house extension meant perhaps for a Buddhist altar room (p76), the unwritten novel, the uncaught carp, the trip untaken. A translation that completes sentences, assigns speakers the Japanese leaves floating, or explains why B stopped the tattoo has committed Berman's clarification in exactly the place this text forbids it. Equally, do not prettify the imagery in the lyrical passages: 'sinful snow-shavings', an owl's eyes in the light, 'goose-down' scattering of his grand phrases — these are meant to be a little too much, and their excess, kept, is what makes the puncturing funny and then, briefly, sad.

A note on limits: the period surface (historical kana, Taishō diction) should not be answered with English archaism. Taki's world — buses, telephones, restaurants, harmonicas playing 'Ai Ai Ai' and 'Valencia', a Tokyo March — was modern to itself. The English should be modern enough to let the comedy move, with its formality carried in sentence shape rather than in thee-and-thou colouring. I cannot settle from the text alone how far Makino intends Taki as self-portrait, and the reading does not need it: the narration's evenness — it never once calls him lazy, dishonest or absurd outright — works whether the target is the author, a friend, or a type. That evenness is the final thing to protect. The last scene's heroic chorus and the absent hero are presented in the same level voice as everything else; the English should end as flatly as it began.
data.say: Reading (prose, crux first), open questions, and voice takes for Makino Shin'ichi's “Snowscape” (雪景色, 1927).

voice_takes.label: Level narration, live wires (recommended)
voice_takes.line:
The house drafts in this take unless the editor picks another; it is the one that keeps all four registers distinct while letting the narration stay dead level, which is what the crux requires. English that would be wrong for it: any archaising patina; any dialect borrowed from a specific English-speaking place for A and B; any softening of the wife into warmth or hardening of her into shrewishness; elegant variation where the Japanese repeats; and any sentence that tells the reader Taki is ridiculous, since the text never does — it merely lets him order a pond about like a general and then fall half-asleep in the spring breeze of his own importance.

House note, not source evidence: this take was formed from the whole text as given, read once through before drafting; proper names (Taki, Nancy Lee) and the few period song-titles are the only items carried untranslated, and the reading deliberately offers no view on how far Taki is a self-portrait, since the text itself does not settle it and the translation does not need it settled.

voice_takes.label: Sharper satire
voice_takes.line: Narration a touch drier and quicker, Taki's lyric flights rendered with their excess fully audible so the deflations land harder; the wife crisper, the workmen broader. This take makes the comedy unmistakable and would suit readers meeting Makino as a humorist. Its risk is the one named in the crux: a satirical edge in the narration's own diction begins to judge Taki from outside, and the brief sadness of the snow passage — a man who suspects his whole inner life is a botched picture, and flees it — can shrink into a punchline. Wrong for it: caricature; workmen as clowns rather than as the story's only competent people.

voice_takes.label: Warmer, more lyrical
voice_takes.line: Narration allowed a dreamier grain, sentences lengthened slightly in the reverie passages, Taki's voice closer to the narrator's so we inhabit the 'dream' before it is punctured; the marriage played with more visible affection, the ending's flatness kept but felt as melancholy. This take honours the fact that the snow vision, however disproportionate, is the most alive writing Taki does in the story. Its risk is ennoblement: prettified, the reveries stop being slightly too much, the carp-hunt loses its mud, and the story becomes a wistful portrait of a dreamer instead of an account of a man whose dreaming is precisely how he avoids everything. Wrong for it: sentimentality about the father and the song; any glow added to the final absence.
